lessonTitle: Surgical Admissions and the Operating Theatre: Pre-, Intra- and Postoperative Roles

blocks.text: A 24-year-old man with 18 hours of migrating abdominal pain, a temperature of 37.9 C and tenderness in the right iliac fossa is waiting for a decision at 03:00. The registrar asks the student, 'Does he need an operation tonight, and what will we check before the knife touches skin?' Those two questions, whether to operate and how to make operating safe, are the heart of this unit.

blocks.markdown: **Assessing a surgical admission.** Start as for any acute admission: ABCDE assessment and resuscitation first, then a focused history (onset, site, character, progression, associated symptoms, previous surgery, medicines including anticoagulants, allergies, last oral intake) and examination (vital signs, abdominal signs such as guarding, rebound and rigidity, hernial orifices, rectal or other examination as indicated). Initial tests are chosen to answer the surgical question: bloods (including group and save), urine, imaging (erect chest X-ray for free gas, ultrasound or CT as appropriate). Provide analgesia, intravenous fluids and keep the patient nil by mouth until a decision is made, following local guidance for drugs and doses.

blocks.title: ASA physical status
blocks.text: The American Society of Anesthesiologists grading summarises pre-operative health: I normal healthy; II mild systemic disease; III severe systemic disease; IV severe systemic disease that is a constant threat to life; V moribund, not expected to survive without the operation; VI declared brain-dead organ donor. The suffix E denotes emergency surgery. It is a broad descriptor of fitness, not a risk score on its own.

blocks.markdown: **Operate or treat conservatively?** The decision balances the benefit of operating against the risk of the operation and the effectiveness of non-operative care. Features that usually mean urgent surgery include generalised peritonitis, free intraperitoneal gas after perforation, strangulated or ischaemic bowel, uncontrolled bleeding and abscess or collection not amenable to drainage. Conditions that may begin conservatively include adhesional small bowel obstruction without peritonitis or ischaemia (nil by mouth, intravenous fluids, decompression if vomiting, close review with explicit criteria for surgery) and some uncomplicated presentations in high-risk patients. The patient's wishes, capacity, frailty, comorbidity and the surgeon's experience all feed into a shared decision.

blocks.title: Worked example 1: deciding on the 24-year-old with right iliac fossa pain
blocks.prompt: A 24-year-old man has 18 hours of migrating periumbilical-to-right-iliac-fossa pain, anorexia, a temperature of 37.9 C, a pulse of 96/min and localised tenderness with guarding in the right iliac fossa. White cell count and CRP are raised. He is otherwise fit and takes no medicines. Decide the plan.

steps.text: Resuscitate and assess: obtain IV access, bloods and a group and save, give analgesia and fluids, keep him nil by mouth. He is stable (no shock), so there is time for an organised plan.

Form the differential: acute appendicitis is the leading diagnosis. Others include mesenteric adenitis, terminal ileitis (for example Crohn disease), gynaecological or urological pathology (consider urine analysis), and testicular pathology (examine the testes).

Decide operative or conservative: localised peritonism with raised inflammatory markers indicates appendicitis requiring surgical review; imaging (for example ultrasound or CT, depending on local pathway) may be used to confirm if the diagnosis is unclear. Appendicectomy is the usual definitive treatment; antibiotic-only treatment may be an option in selected uncomplicated cases after discussing risks and recurrence, according to current guidance.

Prepare: confirm fasting and allergies, check consent is valid and recorded by an appropriately trained person, mark the site if relevant, give prophylactic antibiotics per local policy (agents and doses checked against BNF and local guidance), and book theatre with the anaesthetist informed.

blocks.answer: He is fit (ASA I or II-E) with probable uncomplicated appendicitis: the usual plan is resuscitation and surgical review with a view to appendicectomy, with antibiotic-only treatment as a discussed alternative in selected cases.

blocks.markdown: **Sterile technique in theatre.** The principle is to keep the surgical field free of micro-organisms. The team performs a surgical scrub (nails, hands and forearms) with antiseptic, dries with a sterile towel, puts on a sterile gown and gloves without touching the outer surfaces with bare skin (closed gloving), and moves with the sterile front held in front of the body between chest and waist level. The patient's skin is prepared with an antiseptic (commonly chlorhexidine-alcohol; check allergies and local policy) and allowed to dry before drapes and diathermy (to avoid fire risk). If sterility is broken, the affected item or person is changed.

rows: Front of gown from chest to waist, sleeves to above the elbow
Keep hands in front, above the waist and below the shoulders
Back of gown, below waist, armpits
Never touch or turn your back to the field; pass others face to face or back to back
Drapes on the patient above the table edge
A drape hanging below the table edge is not sterile
Do not reach over them; discard anything dropped or touched by a non-sterile item
Wear properly, cover all hair, change if soiled
blocks.caption: Sterile and non-sterile zones in theatre. Follow your hospital's policy.

rows: Patient identity, site and procedure, consent, site marked, allergy, anaesthesia safety check, pulse oximeter working, airway or aspiration risk, risk of blood loss
All team members introduce themselves by name and role, confirm patient, site and procedure again, antibiotic prophylaxis given, critical events, imaging displayed
Procedure recorded, instrument, swab and needle counts correct, specimens labelled, equipment problems, concerns for recovery
blocks.caption: The WHO Surgical Safety Checklist has three phases; hospitals adapt the wording locally.
The WHO checklist asks whether the risk of blood loss is greater than 500 mL in an adult or 7 mL/kg in a child, to trigger readiness of intravenous access and blood products.

blocks.title: Worked example 2: running the WHO checklist for an elective inguinal hernia repair
blocks.prompt: Mr Q, 58, is having an elective right inguinal hernia repair under general anaesthesia. He is allergic to penicillin (rash). Take the team through each phase.

steps.text: Sign in (before induction): the anaesthetist, nurse and patient confirm his name, date of birth, the procedure and site (right), that consent is signed, that the site is marked, and that he is allergic to penicillin so alternative antibiotic prophylaxis is used according to local policy. The pulse oximeter is attached and working. Airway risk is assessed, and blood loss risk is below the threshold (500 mL in an adult).

Time out (before incision): each person says their name and role. The surgeon states the procedure, side and expected critical steps; the anaesthetist states any concerns; the nurse confirms sterility and equipment. The team confirms antibiotic prophylaxis was given within the previous 60 minutes and imaging is not needed.

Sign out (before he leaves theatre): the nurse reads out the procedure recorded, confirms the instrument, swab and needle counts are correct and that any specimen is labelled. The team states recovery concerns, such as pain management and anticoagulation.
Any 'no' answer pauses the process until resolved. The checklist is a communication tool that must be spoken aloud, not ticked silently.

blocks.answer: Three spoken phases, each with defined checks. A discrepancy (for example a wrong site) stops the procedure until corrected.

blocks.markdown: **The student in theatre.** Introduce yourself to the team, state your level, and read the patient's notes beforehand. Wear appropriate theatre clothing, wash or scrub only if invited and taught, and remain outside the sterile field unless gowned and gloved. If you feel unwell, tell the scrub nurse or surgeon at once, step back from the sterile area and sit or lie down; do not wait until you faint. Patient dignity, confidentiality and the sterile field are priorities. Ask questions when appropriate and take opportunities to observe and help under supervision.

blocks.title: Consent and the student
blocks.text: Consent must be obtained by someone with the appropriate knowledge of the procedure and its risks, usually the surgical team, and be voluntary and informed. A student may observe, gather history, and, under direct supervision and with the patient's agreement, take part in the consent conversation within their competence. If you do not understand the procedure well enough to explain the risks, you must not take consent; say so and involve your supervisor. Patients may refuse student involvement without affecting their care.

items: Assess ABCDE first, then decide operative or conservative using the clinical picture, tests and patient preferences.
Record ASA grade and frailty or comorbidity to inform anaesthetic and surgical risk.
Use the three-phase checklist aloud: sign in, time out, sign out.
Keep sterile zones sterile; step back if you feel unwell.
Seek help whenever consent or competence is in doubt.

points: A surgical admission begins with resuscitation, then a focused history, examination and targeted tests to answer the question: operate now, optimise, or treat conservatively.
Features such as peritonitis, free gas, ischaemia and uncontrolled bleeding point to urgent surgery; others can be observed with defined review criteria.
Sterile technique and the WHO checklist (sign in, time out, sign out) are standard safeguards; any doubt pauses the procedure.

Students observe and assist within competence, do not take consent for procedures they cannot explain, and speak up if unwell or concerned. Doses and regimens must be checked against current BNF, NICE and local guidance.

questions.stem: At which point in the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist are patient identity, site, procedure and consent first confirmed?

options.text: Sign in, before induction of anaesthesia
Time out, immediately before skin incision only
Sign out, before leaving theatre
After the operation in the recovery area

questions.correctOptionText: Sign in, before induction of anaesthesia

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the first phase is before induction, so errors are caught before anaesthesia.
distractorRationale.b: Time out repeats the confirmation; it is not the first check.
distractorRationale.c: Sign out concerns counts, specimens and recovery plans.
distractorRationale.d: After the operation is too late to prevent a wrong-site error.

questions.explanation: Sign in is the first phase and happens before anaesthesia is induced, allowing the patient to take part. Confirmation is repeated at time out for a second line of defence.

questions.stem: Which check belongs to the sign out phase of the checklist?

options.text: Confirmation that the instrument, swab and needle counts are correct and specimens are labelled
Introduction of all team members by name and role
Confirmation that antibiotic prophylaxis was given
Confirmation that the patient's allergies are known

questions.correctOptionText: Confirmation that the instrument, swab and needle counts are correct and specimens are labelled

distractorRationale.a: Correct: counts, specimen labelling and recovery plans are checked at the end.
distractorRationale.b: Introductions are part of time out.
distractorRationale.c: Antibiotic prophylaxis is confirmed at time out or sign in.
distractorRationale.d: Allergy checks are part of sign in.

questions.explanation: Sign out closes the loop before the patient leaves theatre by checking counts, specimens and equipment and by planning recovery. Introductions and allergy checks belong to the earlier phases.

questions.stem: A scrubbed surgeon's gloved hands drop below the level of the operating table while they are talking. What should happen?

options.text: The hands are considered contaminated and the gloves are changed before touching the field
Nothing, because the gloves are sterile
Wipe the gloves with a non-sterile towel
Continue but avoid touching the wound

questions.correctOptionText: The hands are considered contaminated and the gloves are changed before touching the field

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the sterile zone is above the waist and below the shoulders in front of the body; below the table is not sterile.
distractorRationale.b: Gloves lose sterility if they go below the sterile zone.
distractorRationale.d: Contaminated hands must not approach the field.

questions.explanation: Sterile areas are defined by position. Anything below the waist or table level is unsterile, so a hand that falls there must be re-gloved or the person must rescrub as per local policy.

questions.stem: You are scrubbed and gowned as a student assisting in theatre and begin to feel light-headed. What should you do?

options.text: Tell the scrub nurse or surgeon immediately, step away from the sterile field and sit or lie down
Stay still and wait for the feeling to pass without telling anyone
Lean on the sterile instrument table for support
Remove your gloves and walk out without saying anything

questions.correctOptionText: Tell the scrub nurse or surgeon immediately, step away from the sterile field and sit or lie down

distractorRationale.a: Correct: early communication and stepping back protects you and the sterile field.
distractorRationale.b: Delay risks fainting onto the patient or the sterile area.
distractorRationale.c: Leaning on the table contaminates it.
distractorRationale.d: Leaving without telling anyone creates confusion and risk.

questions.explanation: Students who feel faint should communicate promptly and move away before collapse. Safety of the patient and the sterile field comes before completing the observation.

questions.stem: The surgeon asks you, a final-year student, to obtain consent from a patient for a laparoscopic procedure whose risks you cannot explain. What is the best response?

options.text: Explain that you are not able to take consent for this procedure, ask the surgeon or another competent clinician to do so, and offer to observe or assist
Take consent using a standard form without discussing details
Ask the patient's relative to sign for them
Tell the patient the operation is routine and not to worry

questions.correctOptionText: Explain that you are not able to take consent for this procedure, ask the surgeon or another competent clinician to do so, and offer to observe or assist

distractorRationale.a: Correct: consent must be informed, and the person taking it must understand the procedure.
distractorRationale.b: Consent without discussion of material risks is not valid.
distractorRationale.c: Relatives cannot consent for a patient with capacity.

questions.explanation: Consent requires information about the nature, benefits, risks and alternatives. A student who lacks the knowledge must decline and involve a competent supervisor, while observing the conversation can be a good learning opportunity.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with a previous laparotomy has colicky abdominal pain, vomiting and distension for 12 hours. He is haemodynamically stable, the abdomen is soft and non-tender, the lactate is normal and CT shows small bowel obstruction with a transition point and no signs of ischaemia or free gas. Which initial plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Conservative management: nil by mouth, intravenous fluids, nasogastric decompression if vomiting, close monitoring and defined criteria for urgent surgical review
Immediate laparotomy regardless of findings
Oral laxatives and discharge
Intravenous antibiotics alone and routine review in 48 hours

questions.correctOptionText: Conservative management: nil by mouth, intravenous fluids, nasogastric decompression if vomiting, close monitoring and defined criteria for urgent surgical review

distractorRationale.a: Correct: adhesional obstruction without peritonitis or ischaemia is usually managed initially without surgery with close review and clear triggers (such as peritonism, rising lactate or deterioration).
distractorRationale.b: Operating in the absence of any urgent indication exposes him to unnecessary risk.
distractorRationale.c: Laxatives are unsafe in a mechanical obstruction.
distractorRationale.d: A long delay in review risks missing strangulation.

questions.explanation: Uncomplicated adhesional obstruction can often be treated conservatively because many cases resolve, but only with frequent review and explicit triggers for surgery. Local pathways and current guidance should be followed.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man has sudden severe abdominal pain, a board-like rigid abdomen, a heart rate of 118/min and free air under the diaphragm on an erect chest X-ray. What is the correct plan?

options.text: Resuscitate and arrange urgent senior surgical review for emergency laparotomy; do not wait for further non-essential investigations
Observe overnight with oral analgesia
Arrange an outpatient colonoscopy
Treat with antacids and discharge

questions.correctOptionText: Resuscitate and arrange urgent senior surgical review for emergency laparotomy; do not wait for further non-essential investigations

distractorRationale.a: Correct: generalised peritonitis with free gas indicates perforation and needs urgent surgery.
distractorRationale.c: Colonoscopy is unsuitable and unsafe in perforation.

questions.explanation: A rigid abdomen with tachycardia and free gas strongly suggests a perforated viscus. The priority is resuscitation, early antibiotics per local guidance and prompt surgery.

questions.stem: An 18 kg child is booked for surgery. The WHO checklist uses a blood loss threshold of 7 mL/kg for children. Calculate the volume in mL above which the anticipated blood loss would require blood-readiness preparation.
questions.explanation: Threshold = 7 mL/kg x 18 kg = 126 mL. For adults the corresponding checklist figure is 500 mL. Exceeding the threshold prompts the team to ensure adequate intravenous access and availability of blood products.

questions.stem: A medical student may obtain consent for any operation as long as the patient is willing to sign the form.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Consent must be informed, and the person taking it must understand the procedure and its risks. A student who cannot explain the procedure must not take consent but may observe or assist under supervision.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old frail man with ischaemic heart disease, type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease has had 2 days of right upper quadrant pain and fever. Ultrasound shows acute cholecystitis. He is haemodynamically stable. Discuss how you would assess his fitness and decide between operative and conservative management, and what you would need to do to obtain valid consent.
markingGuide: Resuscitate and assess severity: ABCDE, fluids, analgesia, blood cultures and antibiotics per local protocol (doses checked against BNF and local guidance), bloods and monitoring
Assess risk: ASA grade, cardiac and renal comorbidity, frailty, medicines (anticoagulants, antidiabetic agents), functional status; request anaesthetic review

Options: early laparoscopic cholecystectomy if fit; conservative antibiotic treatment with delayed operation; percutaneous cholecystostomy for high-risk patients; select by severity, risk and response, with senior surgeon and anaesthetist input
Shared decision: capacity assessment, discuss benefits, risks, alternatives and the option of doing nothing; consider his wishes and any treatment-escalation decisions
Consent: should be taken by a clinician who understands the procedure, be voluntary and informed, and documented; a student may observe or assist under supervision but should not take consent alone
Pre-operative preparation: fasting, diabetic and renal management, VTE prophylaxis, WHO checklist at theatre
questions.explanation: A strong answer combines acute assessment, risk stratification, a justified choice between several options and a valid consent process. The decision should be shared and clearly documented. Drug choices must be verified against current guidance.
